title: Editorial vs Bold Typography
lede: Both are pages where type is the entire design. One controls how far a line may run; the other controls how large a word may get.
verdict: Editorial caps the measure — 17 characters for the headline, 46 for the standfirst. Bold typography caps nothing and pushes size instead: clamp(3rem, 10.5vw, 7.2rem) at line-height 0.86, in pure black on pure white.
brief: Editorial is a reading style. The headline is 17ch and the standfirst 46ch, a serif display face over a sans body, and the sections are divided by 1px rules rather than cards. Nothing about it is loud; the whole design is the argument that a line of text has a correct length.

Bold typography is a display style. The headline goes to 7.2rem on wide screens with line-height 0.86, letter-spacing tight enough that words nearly touch, and a 12ch measure that forces three or four lines out of a short sentence. There is no second colour, no image, no card: the page is black text on white, and the only variable is scale.
whenA: The page is read in sequence and the reader should never lose their place
There is a deck or standfirst — a real one, not a subtitle repeating the headline
The content is long enough that fatigue is the enemy, not attention
whenB: The page has one sentence to deliver and no body copy worth reading
The brand is confident enough to spend an entire screen on four words
You want scale to do the work that imagery would normally do
promptDelta: Give the model a measure for editorial (17ch, 46ch) and a scale for bold typography (clamp up to 7rem, line-height under 0.9). Asked for "big bold type" without a line-height, a model will keep 1.5 and the block will look like a poster with the air let out of it. Asked for "editorial" without a measure, you get the browser default of roughly 140 characters — twice what a reader can track.
